title: Marx: Alienation
keyWorks: The German Ideology (1845–1846, with Friedrich Engels)
summary: As a young man, Karl Marx wrote manuscripts about how a person can become a stranger to themselves — "alienated". He believed that people come into their own through free, creative activity and through their connections with others, and that when work and life are arranged so that this is impossible, people suffer — and often think it is their own fault.
onEmotions: The young Marx saw the human being as a "species-being" — a creature that lives in connection with others and expresses itself through activity. For him feelings are not only inner states but also responses to how our life is arranged: work, money, relationships. Many painful experiences — tiredness, emptiness, loneliness, envy — can be linked to what he called "alienation": when labour, its results and other people become something external and alien to a person. It is an important idea: part of your pain may have not only personal but also social causes. It doesn't cancel your choices, but it lifts needless guilt.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is an understandable feeling, especially when the future feels unstable. The young Marx described a situation in which a person depends on forces they don't control: the market, money, the decisions of distant people. In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 he shows how what people have created begins to rule over them, like an alien power. From this angle you could say that part of your anxiety is a reasonable response to real uncertainty, not just "wrong thoughts" in your head. That can bring relief: you are not simply "too anxious a person" — you live in a world where much really doesn't depend on you. It helps to separate what is in your power from what is determined by circumstances, and not to shoulder the latter.
anxiety.practice: Split your anxiety into two columns: "what depends on me" and "what depends on circumstances and other people". Which column is longer?

fear.text: Fear is a natural response to threat, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. Marx wrote about people whose existence depends on things they have no power over: will there be work, will the money be enough, will you turn out to be "surplus"? In the 1844 manuscripts he bitterly remarks that the demand for people regulates their fate just as the demand for any other commodity does. From this angle you could say that many fears — losing your job, not coping, being unneeded — come not from your weakness but from the way our shared life is organized. Understanding this doesn't remove the fear, but it makes it less lonely: a great many people share the same insecurity, and it is easier to bear when it can be talked about together.
fear.practice: Write down your fear, and then think: who else most likely feels the same? Which of them could you talk to about it?

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and you don't always have to look for a purely personal cause. The young Marx believed that a person needs to express themselves fully: in activity, creativity, connection with others and with nature. He called this our "species-being" — what makes us human. When life is reduced to survival and obligations, this essence finds no outlet, and a person feels impoverished even if outwardly everything is fine. From this angle you could say that sadness is sometimes the voice of your unrealized humanity: the part of you that wants to do, to create and to be with others. It isn't a whim but a longing for a fuller life. It deserves to be heard, not drowned out.
sadness.practice: Remember the last time you did something out of interest, not for the result. What was it — and could you find at least fifteen minutes for it this week?

grief.text: Grief after a loss is one of the deepest experiences there is, and it takes time. The young Marx didn't write about grief directly, but he had an idea that explains a lot: the essence of a human being is the ensemble of their relationships with others. From this angle you could say that we are made of our connections, and when someone close to us leaves, part of us leaves too. Grief is not weakness but an honest reflection of how deeply we are bound to others. Marx himself later lost several of his children, and in a letter he admitted that he was not one of those "great men" who bear any loss easily. It's a reminder: there is nothing unworthy in grief, even for the strongest minds.
grief.practice: Write down which habits, words or ways of seeing the world you took on from the person you lost. That connection goes on living in you.

loneliness.text: Loneliness is a painful feeling, and it doesn't mean there's something wrong with you. The young Marx saw the human being as a deeply social creature: we become ourselves only through others. One of the forms of alienation he described is the alienation of person from person: when people meet mainly as competitors, buyers and sellers, performers of functions, rather than as living beings. From this angle you could say that loneliness is not only your personal failure but also a consequence of how work, cities and the rhythm of life are arranged. That doesn't mean nothing can be done, but it takes away the shame. Marx dreamed of relationships in which people need each other as people, not as means. Such connections often begin with something small.
loneliness.practice: Think of one person with whom you talked not "on business" but simply as one human being to another. Could you write them a couple of lines today?

quote.text: But the essence of man is no abstraction inherent in each single individual. In its reality it is the ensemble of the social relations.
quote.author: Karl Marx

anger.text: Anger is a strong and often justified feeling: it signals injustice. The young Marx was sensitive to how people suffer from conditions they did not create. From this angle you could say that part of your anger is a normal response to real pressure, inequality or humiliation, not a trait of your character. From his idea of the alienation of person from person one can draw a subtler observation, too: tension whose source lies in the very structure of life is often unloaded onto those nearby — a colleague, a neighbour, someone close. Understanding this frees both you and others from some unnecessary guilt. Anger doesn't need to be suppressed; it can be directed at what can actually be changed.
anger.practice: Ask yourself: who am I angry at — and what pressures, what circumstances stand behind this person, perhaps ones we both share?

shame.text: Shame is a very painful feeling, and you don't have to carry it alone. Interestingly, the young Marx remarked in an 1843 letter to Arnold Ruge that shame is a kind of anger turned inward. From this angle you could say that shame is often the energy of disagreement that we have aimed at ourselves instead of seeing where it really belongs. Marx also showed how, in a society where a person's worth is measured by money and success, people begin to be ashamed of poverty, failure, "inefficiency". In the 1844 manuscripts he wrote that money can turn human qualities into their opposites. If your shame is about not earning or achieving "enough", it's worth asking: is this the truth about you, or about a yardstick the world has imposed on you?
shame.practice: Ask your shame: "Whose yardstick are you measuring me by?" Write down where that yardstick came to you from.

quote.text: Shame is a kind of anger which is turned inward.
quote.author: Karl Marx

guilt.text: Guilt is a heavy feeling, and it matters to understand where it's appropriate and where you're carrying a needless burden. The young Marx showed that many of life's circumstances — lack of time, money, strength, work you're forced to do — are created not by one person but by the whole system of social relations. In the 1844 manuscripts he describes how a person in alienated labour controls neither their activity nor its fruits. From this angle you could say that part of your guilt — for example, for not getting enough done, not caring or earning "enough" — may be guilt for things that weren't entirely up to you. This doesn't cancel responsibility where it truly is yours. But it helps you distinguish: where can I act differently, and where am I carrying someone else's load?
guilt.practice: Write down what you blame yourself for, and mark which part of it is in your hands and which is determined by conditions you didn't choose.

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant, but very understandable. The young Marx noticed that in a world where a person's status and worth are measured by property, envy becomes almost inevitable. In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts he writes that private property breeds envy of the richer and a desire to "level everyone down". Interestingly, he considered this response immature: envy merely turns the same logic of "having" upside down without going beyond it. There, too, he bitterly remarks that the less you are, the more you have. His ideal is not to "have more" but to "be" more fully: to develop your abilities, senses, relationships. From this angle envy can hint at what you lack, but it's worth asking: do I need this to live more fully, or so as not to lose in comparison?
envy.practice: Ask yourself: will what I envy make my life fuller — or just ease the feeling that I'm "worse"? Write down your answer honestly.

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are heavy states, and they don't mean you are a bad or lazy person. The young Marx described alienation from one's own activity: when work is done not because it expresses you but only as a means of survival. In such labour, he wrote, a person does not freely develop their physical and mental energy but mortifies themselves. From this angle you could say that emptiness often appears where we have long been doing things we don't feel are our own. It's not an emptiness inside you, but the trace of a gap between you and what fills your days. Marx believed that a person comes alive in "free, conscious activity". Even a small island of such activity can bring back a sense of being alive.
emptiness.practice: Think of an activity in which you used to lose track of time. Could you give it at least ten minutes this week?

confusion.text: Confusion often arises when the world changes faster than we can understand it. Marx saw this clearly: he wrote about a time when old ways of life were collapsing and new ones had not yet formed. From this angle you could say that confusion is not a personal inability but a natural response to rapidly changing conditions of work, relationships and values. Marx also taught us to look at life historically: what seems "natural" and eternal actually took shape at a particular time and can change. That is liberating. If you feel confused, perhaps you have simply noticed that the familiar rules are not so unshakable after all. It's unpleasant, but it is also the beginning of a clearer view — and of your own choice.
confusion.practice: Write down one "that's how it's done" that is confusing you right now. Where did it come from, and is it really binding for you?

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are not a weakness of character but a response to a real load. The young Marx described this state with striking precision. In the 1844 manuscripts he speaks of "alienated labour": when work doesn't express a person but only drains their strength, they feel like themselves only outside it. Labour becomes external, forced, and all that remains after it is exhaustion. From this angle burnout is not proof that you "can't handle it" but an understandable response to activity in which you yourself are barely present. This can lift some of the guilt: it isn't only about you. And it suggests a direction: protect the time in which you are "at home" in yourself, and look for something in your work that you can make your own.
fatigue.practice: Notice today the moments when you feel "at home" in yourself. What do they have in common?

quote.text: The worker therefore only feels himself outside his work, and in his work feels outside himself. He feels at home when he is not working, and when he is working he does not feel at home.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, "Estranged Labour"

boredom.text: Boredom may seem trivial, but sometimes something important hides behind it. The young Marx wrote about labour reduced to the monotonous repetition of the same operations, engaging neither a person's mind nor their feelings. From this angle you could say that boredom is the protest of your many-sided nature against monotony. Marx believed that humans are by nature versatile: we want to think, to work with our hands, to talk with others and to create. So boredom is not your shortcoming but a hint: some part of you lacks room. In The German Ideology Marx and Engels even dreamed of a life in which one could hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening and criticize after dinner.
boredom.practice: Which of your abilities have you not used for a long time — with your hands, your head or with people? How could you give it a little room this week?

joy.text: Joy is a wonderful feeling, and the young Marx was no ascetic about it. In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts he writes that a person affirms themselves in the world through all their senses — sight, hearing, taste, love. These "human senses" develop together with culture: the musical ear, the eye that feels the beauty of form. From this angle joy is a moment when your senses are alive at full strength: you truly see, hear, delight. Marx criticized a world in which the "sense of having" crowds out all the other senses. That is why joy unconnected with possession — from music, nature, an encounter — is especially precious: in it you are fully human.
joy.practice: Choose one sense — sight, hearing, taste or touch — and give yourself over to it completely for a minute. What do you notice that you hadn't noticed before?

quote.text: The forming of the five senses is a labour of the entire history of the world down to the present.
quote.author: Karl Marx

love.text: Love and tenderness are the most alive things in us, and the young Marx wrote about them with surprising warmth. In the 1844 manuscripts, in the passage on the power of money, he shows how money substitutes for human qualities and relationships: you can get almost anything for it, but not real love. Against this he sets a way of life in which a person relates to the world and to others "humanly". From this angle tenderness is the area of life where alienation retreats: you give not a function or a service, but yourself. For Marx love is one of the chief expressions of human essence, not a commodity. That is why your tenderness is valuable in itself, regardless of what it "brings in".
love.practice: Remember the last thing you shared with someone close "just because" — not out of obligation. How did it feel?

quote.text: Assume man to be man and his relationship to the world to be a human one: then you can exchange love only for love, trust for trust, etc.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, "The Power of Money"

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling, and the young Marx has a thought that makes it deeper. He emphasized that the human being is a social creature: almost everything we have — language, knowledge, things, even our refined senses — was created by the labour of many other people. Even when you think alone, he wrote in the manuscripts, you use a language given to you by society, and your activity remains social. From this angle you could say that gratitude is the recognition of an invisible web of people who support your life: those who grew the bread, built the house, taught you to read. Such gratitude doesn't diminish you, it connects you: you are part of a great shared undertaking.
gratitude.practice: Look at one object near you and try to imagine how many people took part in its coming to you. What do you feel?

hope.text: Hope sustains us, and Marx, for all his sober view of the suffering of his time, was a thinker of hope. His idea of alienation contains a promise: what people have created, people can also change. If suffering flowed from "eternal human nature", there would be nothing to hope for. But if it is tied to how relationships, work and living conditions are arranged, then they can become different. From this angle you could say that hope is not a naive dream but an understanding that the world can change. It needn't be tied to great upheavals: hope begins where you see that even in your everyday life something is not "like this forever" but could be arranged differently.
hope.practice: Write down one thing in your life that seems to have "always been this way". Could even something small in it change?

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm longing for the past, and there is nothing shameful in it. The young Marx didn't write about nostalgia directly, but from his perspective you could say that we often long not only for a time but for forms of life: a courtyard where everyone knew each other, work that was clear and your own, an unhurried pace. That is, for connections that rapid change has washed away. Marx didn't idealize the past — he saw both want and unfreedom in it. But his idea of an unalienated life helps you understand what is valuable in nostalgia: it points to what we truly need — closeness, meaningful work, your own mark on what you do. This can be sought not only behind you but in the present.
nostalgia.practice: What exactly do you miss from the past — a place, people, a rhythm or a feeling? What might a small piece of it look like in your life today?

craving.text: A sharp "I want it right now" can be very strong, and there's nothing shameful in it. In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts the young Marx noticed something strange: in a world where everything is for sale, needs aren't simply satisfied — they are produced. Everyone, he wrote, tries to create a new need in another so as to place them in a new dependence. From this angle you could say that part of your craving is not only "your weakness": the phone, the cigarette, the drink are designed and sold so that you'll be pulled back again. Marx set against such imposed needs the real ones — for activity, for connection, for being rather than having. A craving is a wave: it rises and falls. You can ride it out without arguing with yourself, and ask what real need it is trying to fill.
craving.practice: When a craving hits, set a timer for five minutes and simply watch it, like the weather. Then ask: "What am I actually missing right now — rest, people, meaning?"

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure but a hard circle that very different people fall into. Marx has a famous phrase about religion as "the opium of the people", and it's often taken as mockery. But in the full text he speaks with compassion: it is "the sigh of the oppressed creature", a consolation in a world with too much pain. From this angle you could say the same of addiction: what life came to be organized around was often a way of enduring something unbearable — loneliness, exhausting work, a sense of being unneeded. Marx added that to call for giving up illusions is to call for changing a condition that needs illusions. So the way out lies not in self-flagellation but in gradually reclaiming what was taken away: connections with people, work in which you recognize yourself.
addiction.practice: Write: "When it all began, it helped me endure…" If you feel like it, think about whom you could talk to about this — someone close, or a mutual-help group where people understand.

quote.text: Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, just as it is the spirit of spiritless conditions. It is the opium of the people.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Introduction (1844)

hangover.text: The morning after is hard: your body aches, and on top of it come anxiety, shame and fragments of memory. It's a very understandable state, and you don't have to scold yourself right now. The young Marx made a bitter observation: a person whose labour is alienated feels free almost only in the simplest functions — eating, drinking, resting — while in work, the most human of activities, they feel like a servant. From this angle you could say that a binge is often an attempt to win back at least a scrap of the freedom that's missing on ordinary days. It's an understandable attempt, but it doesn't give what the person is looking for, and in the morning the bill comes to you. This is not a verdict on your character but a reason to ask: where in your life could there be a freedom that doesn't hurt afterward?
hangover.practice: Drink some water, sit comfortably and gently ask yourself: "What did I really want last night — to unwind, to be with people, to forget?" Write down one word.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a strong and joyful experience: as if anything were possible and the world were wide open. There's no need to dismiss it right away. Marx rarely wrote about such states directly, but in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts he describes what an unalienated person might be like: someone whose senses, abilities and connections with people are developed "in an all-round way", who lives rather than merely survives. From this angle you could say that in a moment of elation you glimpse this fullness of yours for a second: how much energy, desire and possibility there is in you. It's not an illusion but a reminder of what you are capable of. The high won't last forever, and that's normal. But you can keep it as knowledge: this is who I can be when nothing is squeezing me.
euphoria.practice: Write a couple of lines: what exactly seems possible to you right now? This list will be useful on an ordinary day, too — as a reminder of your real desires.

crash.text: The drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a bright evening — can be very unpleasant: the world seems to fade, and you want back what was. This is an understandable reaction, not a sign that something is wrong with you. From the young Marx's perspective you could put it like this: a celebration is a time when a person is briefly "at home" in themselves, and then returns to a routine in which they themselves are barely present. The contrast between these two worlds is what makes the comedown hurt. Marx saw the problem not in the fact that celebrations end, but in the fact that ordinary life can be arranged so poorly. So you can take the comedown as information: it shows the gap between what you want and how your everyday life is set up. That gap can be narrowed little by little — not in a leap, but in small steps.
crash.practice: Name one thing from that high — not a substance or an event, but a quality: lightness, company, laughter. How could you add a grain of it to an ordinary day?

panic.text: A wave of panic is truly frightening: your heart pounds, your breath falters, it seems something terrible is about to happen. First, the main thing: a wave like this usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Marx, of course, didn't write about panic attacks. But from his perspective you could say this: many people live in constant insecurity — about work, money, housing — and for years the body holds that background alarm signal. Marx described how social relations a person didn't choose become an alien, uncontrollable power over them. Panic is not proof that you are "weak". Sometimes it is a body that has been on alert for too long. Right now what matters most is not analysis but support: the ground under your feet, the out-breath, the objects around you.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and feel them. Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath, and name aloud five objects around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — "what's the point of it all", the thought of our finitude — is familiar to very many people, and there's nothing abnormal in it. The young Marx touched on this theme in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts. He wrote that death seems a harsh victory of the species over the particular individual — but added that each of us is part of that species, a "species-being". This means your life is woven into a vast human fabric: the language you speak, the things others have made, what you pass on. From this angle the answer to "what for?" is sought not alone, inside your head, but in connections: in activity that someone else needs, in relationships. The abyss doesn't disappear, but many hands turn out to be near it.
dread.practice: Look around and find three things made by other people that help you live today. Write down whom you silently thank for them.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else lives more interesting lives and you're "in the wrong place" is very common and very tiring. Marx has the concept of "commodity fetishism": in a market world, relations between people begin to look like relations between things, and things seem to radiate value on their own. From this angle you could say that a feed of other people's trips, parties and purchases sells not life but an image of it — packaged like a commodity. Marx also set "having" against "being": the more we measure ourselves by possessions, the poorer we feel. Fear of missing out is not a personal deficiency but a natural response to an environment that deliberately shows you other people's abundance. Real life, for Marx, lies in what you do and with whom, not in what can be seen from outside.
fomo.practice: Recall one recent moment that no one saw or posted but that was truly yours. Write it down.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are exhausting and hard to resist. In Capital Marx wrote with great indignation about how the working day eats up the time a person needs to live — including sleep. He noted that capital tends to reduce even healthy sleep to the minimum needed just to work again tomorrow. From this angle you could say that night-time thoughts about work, money and unfinished tasks are not personal disorganization but a trace of how hard it is today to draw a line between work time and your own time. Your sleep is your time, and you have a right to it. You don't have to solve everything at night; it's enough to set your thoughts aside until morning.
sleepless.practice: Keep a sheet of paper nearby and write down each worrying thought in a single line, marked "for the morning". Then turn your attention to the weight of the blanket and the feel of the pillow.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: trust collapses, and with it part of your picture of the world. This pain is legitimate. In the Manifesto Marx bitterly described how the market era "drowned" many human bonds "in the icy water of egotistical calculation", leaving no other bond between people than naked self-interest. And in the 1844 manuscripts he dreamed of a world where "trust can be exchanged only for trust". From this angle you could say: when you are betrayed, two logics often collide — the logic of relationship and the logic of gain, fear, competition. This doesn't excuse the act and doesn't oblige you to forgive. But it helps you avoid concluding that no one can be trusted. Your ability to trust is not naivety but the very human bond that Marx considered the greatest wealth.
betrayal.practice: Name one person whose trust in you, and yours in them, is still alive. Think about what makes that bond different.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is an agonizing mix of fear of loss, hurt and insecurity. Almost everyone knows it. The young Marx made an observation that can apply here too. He wrote that private property has made us "stupid and one-sided": it seems to us that an object is ours only when we possess it. From this angle you could say that jealousy partly speaks the language of property: "he's mine", "she's mine". But the person you love is not a thing but a living subject with their own freedom. Marx considered truly human a relationship in which love can be exchanged only for love. That doesn't mean your jealousy is wrong or that you should be ashamed of it. It shows how dear the person is to you. It's just that you can place another question beside it: not "how do I hold on?" but "what is alive between us?"
jealousy.practice: Try rewriting one jealous thought without the word "mine". What remains when you speak about the person rather than about ownership?

quote.text: Private property has made us so stupid and one-sided that an object is only ours when we have it.
quote.author: Karl Marx

resentment.text: An old grudge is heavy: you carry it for years, and it quiets down only to flare up again. It almost always arises where there was real injustice. In the preface to Capital Marx made an important caveat: he treats people as "personifications" of economic relations, and so is least of all inclined to hold the individual responsible for relations whose creature he remains. From this angle you could say: part of what hurt you came not only from a particular person's ill will but also from the situation — the hierarchy, need, pressure within which they acted. This doesn't relieve them of responsibility and doesn't require forgiveness. But sometimes it helps to see the wider picture — and loosen a little the knot you are holding alone.
resentment.practice: Describe the grudge in two columns: "what the person did" and "in what circumstances it happened". Don't decide anything — just look at both columns.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and it needs time. The young Marx wrote about love with a tenderness surprising in an economist. In the 1844 manuscripts he says that in a human world love can be exchanged only for love, and if your love does not call forth love in return, it is powerless — a "misfortune". It matters that he calls it a misfortune, not a disgrace. Rejection or a breakup doesn't prove you are "not good enough"; love can't be earned like a salary, and it can't be bought — that is its human dignity. From this angle your pain is evidence that you treated the other as a person, not as a function. That is valuable, even when right now it only hurts.
heartbreak.practice: Write one sentence about what you are able to give in love. That ability stays with you even after a breakup.

impostor.text: The fear that you're about to be "exposed" is agonizing — and it is often familiar precisely to conscientious people. Marx described how, in alienated labour, a person loses their connection to the result of their work: the product becomes alien, as if someone else had made it. From this angle you could say that impostor syndrome partly comes from here: when the value of your work is determined by the market, by bosses, by metrics, it's hard to feel it as your own and to believe you've earned it. On top of that, the market constantly demands that you prove you're "worth" your price — and that pressure is easy to mistake for an inner truth about yourself. This is not your personal deficiency but an understandable effect of your environment. It helps to reconnect with the process: to remember what exactly you did with your own hands and head.
impostor.practice: Take one piece of your recent work and list three concrete actions you did yourself. Don't evaluate — just record them.

self_hatred.text: When an inner voice keeps insisting you're worthless, it hurts very much. That voice is wrong, even if it sounds convincing. The young Marx wrote that under alienation a person becomes a stranger not only to their labour but to themselves. A society that measures people by productivity, price and success easily plants a strict appraiser inside us. From this angle you could say that the inner critic often speaks not in your voice but in the voice of the market: "you didn't do enough", "not efficient enough", "you're losing to others". Marx believed a person is valuable as a living being able to feel, create and be with others — not as a commodity. You don't have to win the argument with your inner critic; it's enough to notice that its yardsticks are borrowed and that you are more than its report.
self_hatred.practice: Write down your inner critic's most frequent phrase and ask: "Where did I get this yardstick? Who used to judge me this way?"

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy feeling: it seems nothing depends on you. It deserves respect, because it often reflects real limits. Marx put it very precisely: people make their own history, but not as they please — in circumstances they did not choose. Both halves of the sentence matter. The first reminds you: you are not nothing, your actions mean something. The second lifts needless guilt: if you can't change everything, that's not your personal failure — the circumstances really are strong. From this angle helplessness can be accepted as an honest acknowledgment of limits rather than a verdict. Within those limits there almost always remains something small that can be done — especially together with others.
helplessness.practice: Draw two circles: "what doesn't depend on me" and "what depends on me at least a little". Find one tiny action for today in the second circle.

quote.text: Men make their own history, but they do not make it as they please; they do not make it under self-selected circumstances, but under circumstances existing already, given and transmitted from the past.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte (1852)

procrastination.text: "I can't get started" is not laziness, even though that's what we're often taught to call it. The young Marx described a strikingly familiar phenomenon. Alienated labour, he wrote, does not belong to the person; it is external and forced, and so, as soon as the compulsion disappears, people flee from it like the plague. From this angle you could say that procrastination is often an honest response to a task in which you yourself are absent: the meaning is unclear, the result belongs to someone else, the control is in other hands. That doesn't mean the task doesn't need doing. But it changes the question from "what's wrong with me?" to "what makes this task feel so alien?" Sometimes it's enough to find even a small piece of yourself in it — your own method, your own order, your own interest.
procrastination.practice: Ask yourself: "What in this task can I decide?" Choose your first step — the smallest one — and take it in the way that suits you.

quote.text: Its alien character emerges clearly in the fact that as soon as no physical or other compulsion exists, labour is shunned like the plague.
quote.author: Karl Marx
quote.source: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, "Estranged Labour"

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — after a move or emigration — can be very painful: you lose your footing, your familiar language, your people, the very sense of "I belong here". It's a deep loss, and it deserves to be acknowledged. Marx himself lived most of his life as an émigré — in Paris, Brussels, London, often in poverty. In the Manifesto he described an era in which all that is solid and familiar melts away, and people are compelled to face with sober senses their conditions of life and their relations with one another. From this angle you could say that your feeling is not a personal failure to adapt but an experience the modern world imposes on millions. And Marx's thesis about the human being as the "ensemble of social relations" suggests: home is first of all connections. They can be grown again little by little, without giving up the old ones.
uprooted.practice: Name one connection you already have in your new place — a person, a place, a ritual. And one you have kept with your former home.

overload.text: Overload and the endless feed wear you out: your attention is torn into pieces, and there's still no peace. This is not your inability to "stay focused". Marx, of course, never saw a smartphone, but he described a logic you can recognize here: capital needs to keep expanding, turning ever new areas of life into commodities. From this angle you could say that today your attention itself has become a commodity — it is collected, held and sold, and the feed is designed never to end. Marx also wrote that a person is alienated when the product of their activity begins to dominate them. Your minutes spent in the feed turn into someone else's profit. Understanding this lifts some of the guilt and gives back the right to say: my attention is mine, and I can protect it.
overload.practice: For one minute, put your phone out of sight and look at something still. Ask: "What do I want to spend the next half hour of attention on?"

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real can be strange and frightening. It deserves gentle care. Marx has an idea that echoes this experience. In Capital he writes that a commodity, a simple thing, turns out to be full of "metaphysical subtleties": before our eyes, relations between people take on the "fantastic form" of relations between things. The world of prices, brands and screens has, in his words, a phantom-like objectivity. From this angle you could say that the sense of unreality is sometimes linked to living in an environment where much really is mediated and abstract. The way back to the real, for Marx, is the way back to living activity and living people: to what can be touched, made, shared.
unreality.practice: Pick up a simple object and describe it in detail: its weight, temperature, texture. Then think about whose hands once made it.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. It is worth savoring. The young Marx called nature the human being's "inorganic body": we are connected to it not as outside spectators but as part of it. He also wrote that the human senses — the ability to see beauty, to hear music — are not given once and for all but were formed by the whole history of humankind. From this angle your awe before mountains, the sea, a starry sky or a great work is not only a personal impression. Echoing in it is the long labour of countless people who taught the human eye and ear to feel this way. You can simply accept the wonder: in this moment you are living that full, unalienated feeling Marx dreamed of.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with whatever filled you with awe. Then think about whom you'd like to share it with.

relief.text: Relief is a pleasant feeling: something heavy has let go, and you can breathe out. Allow yourself it without reservations. In the third volume of Capital Marx distinguishes the "realm of necessity" — everything that has to be done for the sake of survival — from the "realm of freedom", which begins where such forced labour ends. He believed free time was the main condition for human development. From this angle relief can be understood as a small passage from one realm into the other: the pressure has gone, and once again you have a space that belongs to you. This is neither trivial nor idleness, but what is worth saving your strength for. Don't rush to fill that space with new obligations right away.
relief.practice: Spend the next ten minutes without any tasks from your list. Notice where you are drawn when no one demands anything.

calm.text: Calm and peace are states you want to hold on to. There is nothing in them that needs justifying. In The German Ideology Marx and Engels sketched a utopian image: in a free society one could hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening and criticize after dinner, without ever becoming a hunter, fisherman or critic. The point of this picture is not agriculture but freedom: a person isn't chained to one role and lives in their own rhythm. From this angle your calm can be understood as a moment when, briefly, you are not reduced to a function — worker, performer, debtor. You simply are. This experience is valuable in itself and reminds you what life could be like.
calm.practice: Tell yourself: "Right now I don't have to be anyone." Stay with that for a minute, noticing your breath and the sounds around you.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is one of the most alive states: you want to make, invent, create. The young Marx saw creative activity as the very essence of the human being. He wrote that a human, unlike an animal, creates "according to the laws of beauty", and that in free labour a person recognizes themselves in what they have made. Elsewhere Marx gave a remarkable example: Milton wrote Paradise Lost the way a silkworm produces silk — because it was an expression of his nature, not for money. From this angle inspiration is a moment of unalienated activity, when you do something because it is yours. There's no need to "monetize" it or judge it right away. You can simply allow yourself to create.
inspiration.practice: Give your inspiration ten minutes without purpose or judgment: a sketch, a note, a melody. Don't think about whether "it'll be useful".

quote.text: Milton produced Paradise Lost for the same reason that a silk worm produces silk. It was an activity of his nature.
quote.author: Karl Marx

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is a feeling people rarely admit to, but almost everyone knows it. It doesn't make you a bad person. In the 1844 manuscripts the young Marx described the "estrangement of man from man": when life is set up as constant competition — for a position, a salary, attention — the other person inevitably starts to look like a rival rather than a comrade. From this angle you could say that schadenfreude is often born not of your "wicked nature" but of a logic in which someone else's success feels like your loss and someone else's failure like a small win. Seeing this logic is already a step away from it. You might notice: the joy lasts a moment, and underneath it there is usually weariness from endless comparison. And you might ask yourself in what kind of world you wouldn't have to compete with this person.
schadenfreude.practice: Write: "What am I competing with this person over — and who set the rules of this competition?"

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold feeling, and it isn't easy to admit it to yourself. Don't rush to judge yourself for it. In a playful questionnaire, "Confession" (1865), Marx named as his favourite maxim the old Latin phrase "Nothing human is alien to me", and as the vice he detested most — servility. This suggests an interesting move: contempt sometimes points to a value that has been offended — dignity, honesty, a refusal to grovel. But Marx also showed something else: a society where people are ranked by money and status teaches us to look down on others, or up at them. From this angle you can ask whether your contempt is speaking in someone else's voice — the voice of that hierarchy. Contempt can be taken as a signal without turning it into a verdict on a person.
contempt.practice: Complete the sentence: "What I despise in them is… because what matters to me is…" What is that value?

disgust.text: Disgust is an ancient, bodily feeling: something inside says "no, I don't want to touch this". It can be directed at people, at a situation, even at yourself, and it has a right to exist. The young Marx wrote a great deal about the human senses: he believed our sight, taste and sense of beauty are fruits of a long history, and that under alienated conditions they grow coarse. From this angle disgust at certain situations — at falseness, at work where only the numbers count, at humiliating rules — can be a sign of a living, unspoiled sensibility. And if the disgust is aimed at yourself, it's worth asking: are you looking at yourself through the eyes of the market, as a "defective product"? You are not a product. Disgust points to where you are missing something human.
disgust.practice: Name one thing that disgusts you and ask: "What human quality is being violated here?"

revenge.text: The desire for revenge is an understandable response to pain that was done to you. This feeling doesn't make you cruel: it says you were treated unjustly and that this matters. Marx offered an unusual view of people who cause harm. In the preface to Capital he explained that he deals with individuals only insofar as they are personifications of particular social relations. From this angle you could say: behind the one who hurt you there often stands a whole system of pressures, rules and roles, and revenge against one particular person rarely touches the real cause. This is not an excuse for the offender. It is a way of seeing that you don't have to carry your pain as a personal score to settle. You can hear the desire for revenge as a demand for justice — and look for ways to pursue it that don't multiply harm.
revenge.practice: Write: "What does my hurt really demand — recognition, justice, safety?" One word is already an answer.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — is a very common feeling, and many people know the shame that comes with it. You are not a bad person because it arises. Marx wrote little about family life in a psychological sense, but an important observation follows from his thought: the tiredness, lack of time and money worries that build up during the day don't stay at work — they come home. Marx described in detail how the working day swallows up the time a person needs for living, for rest and for loved ones. From this angle part of the anger that crashes down on your family is actually addressed to the pressure you live under together. This doesn't cancel responsibility for your words, but it lifts needless self-blame and helps you talk to those close to you as allies.
anger_at_loved.practice: After an outburst, ask yourself: "What was pressing on me today before that moment?" Write down at least two things.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is hard, but entirely human. Marx inherited dialectics from Hegel — the view that contradiction is not a mistake but something present in life itself that drives it forward. Things and relationships contain opposites, and development proceeds through their tension, not by eliminating one side. From this angle mixed feelings toward someone close are not a sign that the love is "not real". They reflect the real contradictoriness of the relationship: it holds warmth and dependence, care and burden. You don't have to choose which feeling is "right". You can acknowledge both — and see in their clash a question about how the relationship might change.
ambivalence.practice: Draw two columns: "what I love in them" and "what I can't stand in them". Don't cross anything out; just look at both.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a death, a breakup or a loved one's long illness can be frightening: "How can I feel relief if I loved them?" But relief and love can live together perfectly well. Marx showed how much of human life is spent on hard, exhausting labour. Later thinkers building on him drew attention to the invisible labour of care — nursing the sick, giving support, keeping watch — which hardly anyone counts as work. From this angle your relief is not a betrayal but a natural response of body and soul to the end of an enormous, often overwhelming load. It speaks of how much you carried, not of how little you loved. You can allow yourself both to grieve and to breathe out.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down what you carried all this time: what tasks, worries, sleepless nights. Look at this list with respect for yourself.

indifference.text: Sometimes, where something "should" move you, inside it is quiet and empty. That's frightening, but it doesn't mean you're heartless. The young Marx noted in the 1844 manuscripts that a person weighed down by need and worry stops responding even to the most beautiful things. Feelings are not a constant given: they grow dull when life is reduced to survival, to endless tasks and anxieties. From this angle indifference is often not a character trait but a sign of depletion, the psyche's way of protecting itself from overload. You don't need to shame yourself for "wrong" reactions. It's better to ask how much strength and time you have right now simply to feel. The capacity to respond usually returns when a little room appears.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: "How much room is left in me for feelings this week?" Rate it from 0 to 10, without reproach.

quote.text: The care-burdened, poverty-stricken man has no sense for the finest play.
quote.author: Karl Marx

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a familiar role — is familiar to many, and in itself it says something important. In The German Ideology Marx and Engels dreamed of a society where a person isn't chained to one narrow function: where one could hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon and criticize in the evening, without becoming a "hunter" or a "critic" forever. The picture is deliberately simple, and many scholars see some irony in it, but the thought behind it is deep: a person feels cramped in a single role imposed on them. From this angle your wish to escape may be a longing for a many-sided life rather than a weakness. You don't have to change anything right away. First you can listen for which part of you lacks room.
escape.practice: Write: "If I weren't only… (your role), I would also…" Which one small thing from that is possible this week?

quote.text: …to hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticise after dinner, just as I have a mind, without ever becoming hunter, fisherman, herdsman or critic.
quote.author: Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is "off limits" can be confusing and unsettling. But the feeling itself doesn't yet decide anything about you. The young Marx treated human passions without moralizing: he saw the human being as a sensuous, "suffering" being — that is, one who needs the outer world and other people — and passion as one of its essential powers. From this angle attraction is not a vice but a sign that you are alive and in need of something. It helps to ask what it is really reaching for: this particular person, or something missing from your life — aliveness, recognition, freedom. Understanding doesn't commit you to any action. It simply gives you back your own feeling.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down three words: what you feel near this person or when thinking of them. Which of these is missing from the rest of your life?

quote.text: Passion is the essential power of man energetically bent on its object.
quote.author: Karl Marx

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment is a heavy, draining feeling, and you're not alone in it. Marx showed how, in a society where everything becomes a commodity, people come to feel that they themselves are up for sale. Erich Fromm, who developed Marx's ideas, later called this the "marketing orientation": a person experiences themselves as a commodity whose value depends on how others "rate" them. From this angle you could say your fear of judgment is not only a personal weakness but also a reflection of an atmosphere of constant selection — interviews, likes and ratings. You are not goods in a shop window. In human relationships, Marx wrote, trust is exchanged only for trust, not for a successful "self-presentation".
social_anxiety.practice: Before meeting people, tell yourself: "I'm not going there to sell myself, just to be among people." Notice what changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is one of the most draining states: you want something to hold on to, and there's nothing. In the Manifesto Marx and Engels described the modern era as a time of continuous change, when nothing stays the same for long: professions, cities, the familiar way of life. From this angle you could say that your insecurity is not only a personal inability to "plan everything" but a feeling the era itself produces in millions of people. That can ease the load a little: you are not obliged to single-handedly create a stability the world doesn't provide. Marx named "Doubt everything" as his motto — and perhaps uncertainty can be met not only with fear but with questions: what here depends on me, and what doesn't?
uncertainty.practice: Divide a sheet into two parts: "depends on me" and "doesn't depend on me". Choose one thing from the first part.

quote.text: Constant revolutionising of production, uninterrupted disturbance of all social conditions, everlasting uncertainty and agitation distinguish the bourgeois epoch from all earlier ones.
quote.author: Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, a decision — can be agonizing: time drags, and there's nothing you can do. Marx wrote about alienation as a situation in which the result of your efforts doesn't belong to you, and decisions are made somewhere else, by other hands. From this angle you could say that the heaviness of waiting is also a feeling of powerlessness: you put yourself in, and now the outcome is in someone else's hands — a committee, an employer, an institution. This is not your weakness but a very real dependence. But waiting doesn't have to swallow all your time. Marx valued free activity in which a person recognizes themselves. You can reclaim at least a small piece of time that belongs only to you.
waiting.practice: Choose one small task for today whose result depends only on you, and see it through to the end.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again. It shows that you care. Marx wrote that people make their own history, but not as they please — rather in circumstances they did not choose. From this angle you could say: your past decisions were made not in a vacuum but under the pressure of money, time, others' expectations and what you knew then. Looking back, we see the choice more clearly than we saw it at the time, and we judge ourselves as if the circumstances hadn't existed. Honestly acknowledging them doesn't mean letting yourself off entirely. It means looking at your past as fairly as you would look at someone else's.
regret.practice: Write down a decision you regret, and next to it three circumstances in which you made it at the time.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is one of the deepest forms of pain, and there's nothing shameful in it. The young Marx wrote that human wealth is measured by the extent to which another person — precisely as a person, not as a use or a function — has become a need for us. From this angle your longing is a sign of genuine human connection: what you miss is not services or comforts but this very face, this voice, this way of laughing. Marx believed the essence of a human being lies in their connections with others. So when someone isn't near, it's as if part of you is missing. Longing is the price of real closeness. It doesn't need to be hurried; it can be carried gently.
longing.practice: Write down one trait of this person that you came to know only through closeness. Stay with it for a minute.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from grim news, violence, injustice — speaks of your capacity for compassion. The young Marx called the human being a "species-being": we are connected to all of humanity, and the suffering of others resonates in us for a reason. From this angle your pain is not weakness or "excessive sensitivity" but an expression of that shared human bond. Marx wrote that philosophers have only interpreted the world, but the point is to change it. But no one can change the world alone and in a day. You can carry your part: help a particular person, do something kind nearby. And also protect your strength, so that the pain doesn't turn into burnout. Compassion needs rest, too.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small kind act for someone near you — and afterward allow yourself to put the news aside for at least an hour.

rejection.text: Rejection — being turned down for a job, a friendship, a love — wounds deeply, and that's natural. Marx showed how, in a world where people are constantly being selected, it's easy to start treating a refusal as a verdict on your worth. On the job market a rejection often means only that you didn't fit a narrow function, not that you as a person are not good enough. From this angle you could say: the logic of "selection" carries over into personal life too, and then every "no" feels like an assessment of your whole personality. But a person can't be reduced to the function someone is looking for in them. Marx believed in the richness of human abilities, many of which have no market price at all.
rejection.practice: Write down three of your qualities that have nothing to do with what you were turned down for. Read them aloud.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is a deep, almost childlike feeling, and it deserves gentleness. Marx criticized the idea of the human being as an isolated individual, a "Robinson Crusoe" existing on their own. He believed humans are by nature social beings and simply cannot live fully outside their connections with others. From this angle your fear is not weakness but a reflection of a truth about people: we really do need one another. But there is also a social side: in a world where people are disconnected and support often rests on one or two close people, the fear of losing them becomes especially sharp. You can gradually widen your circle of support — not instead of the person close to you, but alongside them.
abandonment.practice: Draw your "map of support": who and what supports you besides the one main person? Even small points count.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a painful feeling, and your pain is real. The young Marx has a famous passage on love: in a human world love can be exchanged only for love, trust only for trust. It can't be bought, earned through effort, or bargained for. Marx acknowledged that love which calls forth no love in return becomes a misfortune for the one who loves. But a consolation follows from his thought too: the absence of a response doesn't mean you aren't trying "enough" or aren't worth something. Love doesn't obey the logic of merit and payment. Your capacity to love is a precious human power, and it remains yours even when this person can't respond.
unrequited.practice: Write to yourself: "My love was not a payment, and a refusal is not an invoice for my worth." What do you feel as you read this?

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: as if you had been stripped of your dignity in front of others. It is not your fault that you were humiliated. In his questionnaire "Confession" Marx named servility as the vice he detested most, and submission as his idea of misery. He was sensitive to how hierarchies of power and money allow some people to treat others as things. From this angle humiliation speaks not of your insignificance but of an imbalance of power in a situation where you weren't recognized as an equal. It hurts precisely because you feel that a human being must not be treated this way. That feeling is your dignity, which goes on living even when it isn't recognized.
humiliation.practice: Say one sentence aloud to yourself: "I must not be treated this way." Notice where in your body that right resonates.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is a very common and painful feeling. The young Marx wrote that alienated labour makes even a person's own body alien to them: it turns into a means, a tool, rather than a living part of themselves. From this angle one could add: today the body often becomes a "commodity" as well, a shop window constantly compared with models from advertising and social media. Beauty standards are largely created by a market that profits from your dissatisfaction. Marx saw the human being as a sensuous creature whose body is there for living, feeling and touching the world — not for matching a shop window. Your body is not an improvement project but your way of being alive.
body_shame.practice: Name three things your body allowed you to feel or do today. Just note them.

illness.text: Illness, when your body lets you down, knocks the ground from under your feet. It's hard, and you have every right to grieve your former strength. The young Marx emphasized that the human being is a natural, bodily and vulnerable creature, not a machine. He described with bitterness how society values a person by their capacity to work, by how much they can produce. From this angle you could say: in illness it's not only the body that hurts — the feeling "I'm useless", imposed by a world that measures people by efficiency, hurts too. But a person's worth doesn't lie in their productivity. You are no less human when you are lying down, resting, accepting care. Allowing yourself to be vulnerable is also part of being human.
illness.practice: Tell yourself: "Today my task is simply to be." Note one thing you can thank your body for, even a tired one.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy, well-earned feeling. There's no need to hide it. The young Marx believed that a person unfolds in creative activity: in making something, they see themselves in what they have made. Free labour, for Marx, is not just a way to earn money but a way to realize your powers, to make them visible and tangible. From this angle pride is a moment when you recognize yourself in what you've done: here are my efforts, my decisions, my strength, embodied in the world. It is the opposite of alienation. Allow yourself to enjoy this feeling without comparing yourself to others or belittling the result: it is yours.
pride.practice: Look at what you've done and name three of your qualities that are embodied in it.

quote.text: …and he therefore contemplates himself in a world that he has created.
quote.author: Karl Marx

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness for what has gone. It doesn't need "treating". Marx, known as a rigorous economist, was also a passionate reader of Homer, Shakespeare and Aeschylus. In the Introduction to his manuscripts of 1857–1858 he asked a remarkable question: why does Greek art still give us pleasure? And he answered: the childhood of humanity holds an eternal charm for us as a stage that will never return. From this angle you could say that melancholy is a similar feeling: we admire what was and will not come back, and it is precisely its unrepeatability that makes it beautiful. Melancholy is a way of cherishing the past without demanding that it return.
melancholy.practice: Recall a time or place you quietly feel sad about. Name what was unrepeatably beautiful in it.
